title: CCDV-F Mock Exam #14 (Moderate Tier)
description: Full-length 53-question moderate-difficulty simulation for Claude Certified Developer - Foundations (120 minutes). Realistic exam-style mix of easier, medium, and hard scenario questions.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A UI-testing agent attaches one 840 × 560 pixel screenshot to each request. Before writing the ingestion code, the developer estimates the image's context cost using the patch formula from the course. About how many visual tokens does one screenshot use?

options.text: About 600 visual tokens, since the image is 30 patches wide (840 / 28) by 20 tall (560 / 28) and each 28 × 28 patch is one token.
About 50 visual tokens, found by adding the 30 horizontal patches and the 20 vertical patches together to get the patch count.
About 85 tokens, a flat per-image charge that applies to every image regardless of its resolution or the model tier in use.
About 470,400 tokens, with each pixel counted as one visual token, so the total is simply the image's width multiplied by its height.

questions.explanation: The course's formula is ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉ visual tokens, because Claude views an image in 28 × 28 patches. For 840 × 560 that is 30 × 20 = 600 tokens per screenshot. Doing this calculation at design time shows whether a pipeline fits its context budget before any ingestion code is written.

distractor_explanations.B: The patch grid is multiplied, not added: ⌈w/28⌉ × ⌈h/28⌉. Adding the two dimensions badly understates the cost.
distractor_explanations.C: There is no flat per-image charge in the course's model; cost scales with the image's dimensions through the patch formula.
distractor_explanations.D: Claude reads images in 28 × 28 patches, not pixels. Counting pixels overstates the cost by orders of magnitude.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A support assistant on the first-party API lets users ask questions about a 60-page product manual PDF across conversations that often run 30 turns. Today the app re-sends the PDF as base64 in every request. Which input method fits this usage best?

options.text: Convert each page into a PNG and attach the sixty images to each request, because image blocks are cheaper than document blocks.
Reference the manual by a URL on the company's internal wiki, which sits behind single sign-on, so no bytes travel in the request itself.
Upload the manual once via the Files API and reference its `file_id`, so requests carry an ID, not the bytes, as history grows.
Keep sending inline base64, which is the recommended method whenever a document is needed on many turns of one long conversation.

questions.explanation: The Files API is the course's choice when the same image or PDF appears across many requests or turns: upload once, receive a `file_id`, and reference it, so payload overhead drops to near zero as history grows. It is in beta on the first-party API, which this assistant uses. Inline base64 is for one-off inputs, and URL sources must be public and reachable.

distractor_explanations.A: This replaces one repeated payload with sixty repeated ones. The course does not say image blocks are cheaper than documents.
distractor_explanations.B: A URL source must be public and reachable when Claude fetches it. A page behind SSO cannot be fetched.
distractor_explanations.D: Base64 suits one-off inputs. Re-sending the same large file on every turn multiplies payload size and latency.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team is choosing how to send product images to the Messages API for a few different pipelines. Which TWO statements about the image input methods are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A URL source needs the image to be stable, public, and reachable when Claude fetches it, so links behind auth are a poor fit.
The Files API is the right default even for a single one-off image, because the upload step adds no work and no extra call at all.
A URL source is fetched once per API key and then cached by the API, so later requests that cite the same URL skip the fetch entirely.
Inline base64 images skip the visual-token formula, and their encoded bytes are counted at the text rate rather than as image patches.
Inline base64 sends the full encoded payload with every request, so resending the same image many times multiplies request size.

questions.explanation: Each method has a distinct overhead. Base64 carries the full payload on every request, so it suits one-off images. A URL source carries no payload, but the image must be stable, public, and reachable when Claude fetches it. The Files API pays a one-time upload and then sends only a `file_id`, which suits assets reused across requests or turns.

distractor_explanations.B: For a one-off image the course prefers base64, because a separate upload step adds complexity with no payoff.
distractor_explanations.C: The course describes Claude fetching the image at request time. It describes no per-key URL cache.
distractor_explanations.D: The sending method doesn't change how an image is tokenized. Visual tokens come from the patch formula.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A contract-review pipeline was tested on two-page sample PDFs. In production it sends three full contracts, often 150+ pages each, as `document` blocks in one request. Many requests now fail with a validation error before any output is generated. What is the best diagnosis and fix?

options.text: Each document block is missing its required `name` field, which triggers the validation error; adding a name to every block will fix it.
The failures are rate limits caused by the large payloads, so the requests should be retried with exponential backoff and jitter until they succeed.
The API is truncating the oldest document to fit, and the error flags that truncation; reorder the documents so the key contract is sent last.
The combined documents exceed the context window, so the API rejects the input before generating; measure real-size inputs and send fewer pages.

questions.explanation: Images and PDFs use up context budget before Claude reads any of your prompt, and a request whose input is already larger than the window is rejected with a validation error before generation starts. Analogy: an airline checks your suitcase at the gate, and if it is over the size limit it is refused before you board; nobody quietly removes your shoes to make it fit. The fix is to measure token cost on production-scale inputs and keep each request under budget, for example by sending one contract or a page range at a time. The tempting truncation idea fails because the API never silently drops content.

distractor_explanations.A: A document block has no required `name` field; `title` and `context` are optional. The two-page samples worked with the same blocks, so total size is the cause.
distractor_explanations.B: A validation error is a terminal 400-class problem. Retrying the identical oversized request fails the same way every time.
distractor_explanations.C: The API never silently drops content. An oversized input is rejected outright with a validation error before generation.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A mobile expense app lets a user photograph a receipt and then waits on screen for the category label. To cut costs, a developer proposes sending each receipt through the Message Batches API instead of a normal Messages call. What does the course advise?

options.text: Keep the synchronous call, because a user is waiting and batch processing can take hours, so the batch discount doesn't fit.
Use the Batches API but poll it every second, because frequent polling makes the batch finish fast enough for an interactive screen.
Use the Batches API for receipts and stream each batch result back to the phone, which hides the batch latency from the waiting user.
Use the Batches API; a batch containing a single request is returned within a few seconds and still gets the lower batch pricing.

questions.explanation: The course's rule is that batch fits offline, high-volume work where no user is waiting, while a user uploading a photo and expecting an immediate answer needs the synchronous API. Using batch in a user-facing flow passes tests and fails in production because the user is waiting and the batch is not.

distractor_explanations.B: Polling only checks status more often. It does not speed up processing, so the user still waits an unpredictable time.
distractor_explanations.C: Batches don't stream results to a waiting user. Streaming applies to synchronous calls, not to an asynchronous batch.
distractor_explanations.D: Batch completion time is non-deterministic and can take up to 24 hours. It doesn't promise a fast return for small batches.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A retailer runs all workloads on Google Cloud, manages access with Google Cloud IAM, and holds its compliance certifications there. It now wants a Claude-based search assistant. Which platform and versioning approach does the course point to?

options.text: Vertex AI with Google Cloud IAM, regional or global endpoints chosen for residency, and the full model ID pinned in Vertex's format.
Claude in Amazon Bedrock, which has the broadest feature parity, with AWS roles federated to Google identities for access control.
The first-party Claude API with an Anthropic key, which gets new features first and lets the customer's Google certifications carry over.
Google Vertex AI with the `sonnet` alias, so the assistant follows Anthropic's deprecation schedule automatically without a code change.

questions.explanation: The customer's existing cloud usually determines the platform. Vertex AI uses Google Cloud identity, IAM, and billing, offers regional or global endpoints for residency, and should be pinned with the full model ID in Vertex's format, since partner retirement dates differ from Anthropic's schedule.

distractor_explanations.B: Moving a Google Cloud customer to AWS ignores where its identity, billing, and compliance posture already live.
distractor_explanations.C: Certifications don't transfer across platforms. A customer certified on Google Cloud is unlikely to re-certify elsewhere.
distractor_explanations.D: The platform is right but the versioning isn't: an alias moves, and Vertex's partner retirement dates differ from Anthropic's.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A developer wires a Vertex AI client for a Dutch insurer whose data must be processed inside the EU. To avoid capacity errors, the client is configured with the global endpoint and no region. The integration passes all functional tests. What should a code reviewer flag?

options.text: Nothing: Vertex AI processes each request in the same region where the customer's Google Cloud project was first created.
The global endpoint, since it can serve requests outside the EU; residency requires pinning the client to an in-jurisdiction region.
The test coverage: a residency gap would have appeared as a failing functional test if the configuration had been wrong.
The model choice, because EU residency depends on picking a model tier marked as EU-restricted, while the endpoint itself has no effect.

questions.explanation: For GDPR and residency, the course rules out delivery routes where the region of execution cannot be pinned, and it names defaulting to a global endpoint without a region as the common way this breaks. Analogy: ordering from an online store with the option to ship from any warehouse worldwide gets the parcel fastest, but if customs rules say it must come from a domestic warehouse, you have to tick that box yourself; the store won't guess. The fix is pinning the region in the client configuration to a covered jurisdiction. The tempting idea that passing tests proves compliance fails because functional tests never observe where processing happened.

distractor_explanations.A: The course says regional routing must be configured. A global endpoint without a region can serve from outside the boundary.
distractor_explanations.C: Functional tests check behavior, not where data is processed. Residency is a configuration fact that a reviewer must check.
distractor_explanations.D: Residency is set by the delivery route and region in the client, not by choosing a particular model tier.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team measured 160 ms round-trip latency for a candidate platform from their office laptop using a short test prompt. The customer's users are in Singapore and send 40 KB documents. Before committing to the platform, what does the course recommend?

options.text: Re-measure from the customer's region with real payloads, since a laptop test hides the round trip users actually see.
Lower `max_tokens` until the laptop figure falls under the target, since output length is the main latency lever before deployment.
Pick the first-party API by default, because it has the lowest latency from every region thanks to its newer features.
Accept the 160 ms figure; model latency is the same everywhere, and the prompt's token count is what changes the result.

questions.explanation: The course says a latency number is only accurate when measured from the customer's actual region against their actual payload, because a laptop test hides the round-trip penalty that appears where the customer is. A platform in the customer's own region can shorten the round trip, while the first-party API is advantaged on early access to features.

distractor_explanations.B: This optimizes the wrong measurement. The number must first be measured from the customer's region and payload.
distractor_explanations.C: Early feature access is not round-trip speed. An in-region cloud platform often wins on latency.
distractor_explanations.D: Latency depends on where the platform runs relative to the customer, so a laptop number does not transfer.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: Procurement wants to choose the platform with the lowest per-token price for a document-processing workload. The customer's documents live in a different cloud from that platform, and the integration would need a new identity setup. What does the course say about comparing cost?

options.text: Defer the cost comparison until after launch, when production traffic is flowing and real token usage per call can be measured.
Compare total cost per call, including egress, platform fees, and integration effort, since per-token rates are broadly aligned.
Choose the lowest token price; tokens dominate the bill, and egress, fees, and integration effort are one-time costs too small to matter.
Use whichever platform supports prompt caching, because caching makes token cost the same on every platform for any workload.

questions.explanation: Per-token rates are broadly aligned across platforms, and the course says total cost moves on data egress, platform fees, and integration effort. A lower token price can cost more overall once transfer and integration are counted, so the comparison should be total cost per call for the real workload.

distractor_explanations.A: The course says to instrument cost per call per platform and confirm pricing at scoping, not after the choice is locked in.
distractor_explanations.C: The course says total cost moves on egress, platform fees, and integration effort, so a cheaper token can cost more in total.
distractor_explanations.D: Caching lowers repeated-prefix cost but does not erase egress, fees, or integration differences between platforms.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: An architect is preparing a platform comparison that procurement and security teams will review. Which TWO statements about how platforms differ match the course? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Claude Platform on AWS keeps inference inside the customer's AWS boundary, so it satisfies the same residency rules as Claude in Amazon Bedrock.
Compliance certifications are the same on every cloud, so compliance rarely decides placement once latency and cost have been measured.
Per-token rates differ widely between platforms, so the token price is normally the deciding factor in a total-cost comparison of platforms.
A cloud the customer has already certified usually wins on compliance, because a customer is unlikely to re-certify on another cloud for one workload.
The first-party Claude API typically receives new capabilities before they reach other platforms, which is its main advantage on feature access.

questions.explanation: A defensible placement measures three things: latency, compliance, and total cost. The first-party API typically gets new capabilities first, an in-region cloud platform shortens round trips, and the cloud a customer has already certified wins on compliance because re-certifying is unlikely. Analogy: a bakery's flagship store gets new recipes first, but if you already hold a membership card at the branch near home that your employer reimburses, that branch is the one you can actually use. The most tempting wrong statement is the token-price one, but the course says per-token rates are broadly aligned, so egress, fees, and integration decide cost.

distractor_explanations.A: Claude Platform on AWS is accessed through the AWS account but runs inference on Anthropic-operated infrastructure outside the AWS boundary.
distractor_explanations.B: The course says compliance often ends the debate: certifications and audit controls differ by platform and are pass-or-fail.
distractor_explanations.C: The course says token rates are broadly aligned, and total cost moves on egress, platform fees, and integration effort.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A release checklist says every production service must use a pinned model reference. A reviewer flags a service that uses `claude-opus-4-8` because the string has no date suffix, and asks for one to be added. Assuming the course's convention, what is the correct response?

options.text: Replace it with an ARN-style identifier, because ARN-versioned IDs are the fixed-snapshot format on each deployment platform.
For Claude 4.6 and later the model ID alone pins a fixed snapshot; the date-suffix rule applies only to earlier models.
Replace it with the `opus` alias; aliases are the pinned form, and full model IDs are the ones that move to new snapshots.
Agree and append a date suffix, because every model ID needs a date suffix to pin a snapshot, whatever the model generation.

questions.explanation: Every Claude model ID points to a specific snapshot, but the pinning convention changed with the 4.6 generation: for Claude 4.6 and later the model ID alone pins, while earlier models need the ID plus a date suffix. Analogy: in a newer apartment block every flat has a unique number on its own, but in an older complex you also need the building letter to find the right door; adding a letter to the new block's address adds nothing. The reviewer's instinct to pin is right, but the suffix rule belongs to pre-4.6 models, and swapping to the alias would undo the pin entirely.

distractor_explanations.A: ARN-versioned identifiers belong to legacy Bedrock integrations. They aren't a universal pinning format.
distractor_explanations.C: This inverts the rule: aliases move over time, and a pinned full model ID resolves to a fixed snapshot.
distractor_explanations.D: The course says the ID plus a date suffix is required only for pre-4.6 models. For 4.6 and later, the ID alone pins.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A production log shows: `deploy model="opus"`, then `alias advanced -> new opus version (no app change)`, then a parser `KeyError` on a missing field, and finally `rollback attempted -> no pinned prior version retained`. Which remediation addresses the root cause?

options.text: Wrap the parser in a retry loop, treating a `KeyError` after a model update as a transient fault that clears on the next attempt.
Switch the alias from `opus` to `sonnet`, because the Sonnet alias changes less often and is the recommended default for production.
Make the parser tolerant of missing fields and keep the `opus` alias, so future output-shape changes no longer cause errors in production.
Pin the full model ID, keep the prior pinned version as a rollback target, and gate each new version through the eval before promoting it.

questions.explanation: The application never changed; the alias did, and no pinned prior version existed to roll back to. The course's fix is to pin the full model ID so updates are deliberate, keep the prior pinned version so a regression is a rollback rather than a hotfix, and gate new versions through the eval before promotion.

distractor_explanations.A: The output shape changed deterministically. Retrying returns the same shape and does not touch the root cause.
distractor_explanations.B: Any alias is a moving target. Changing which alias is used does not pin anything or create a rollback target.
distractor_explanations.C: This hotfixes the symptom and leaves the unpinned deployment in place, so the next alias move is still a silent change.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team sends 10% of traffic to a new pinned model version, compares its eval score against the pinned baseline, and then promotes or rolls back. In the course's systems lifecycle (requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate, iterate), which phase does this activity belong to?

options.text: Requirements, because the pinned baseline score is a requirement, so comparing against it is part of requirements gathering.
Operate: the activity uses live production traffic, and activities that touch production belong to the operate phase.
Deploy, since that phase pins the version and gates promotion on the eval, which is what a traffic slice against baseline does.
Test, because any activity that runs the eval suite belongs to the test phase, whether or not live production traffic is involved.

questions.explanation: The course maps deploy to pinning the version and gating promotion on the eval, and describes the gate as refusing to move toward full production until the new version clears the eval against the pinned baseline. Test covers evals and unit, integration, and end-to-end checks, while operate covers instrumentation and guardrails in production.

distractor_explanations.A: Requirements capture functional and infrastructure needs. Comparing a rollout against a baseline is a release decision.
distractor_explanations.B: Operate covers instrumenting cost, latency, and errors and enforcing guardrails, not deciding whether a version is promoted.
distractor_explanations.D: Running evals during build-time checks is testing, but gating promotion on the eval is named as part of the deploy phase.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A hospital network wants a Claude feature that processes PHI. It already runs a HIPAA-eligible AWS account. Which TWO delivery routes does the course describe as acceptable for PHI? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A cloud-mediated route through AWS Bedrock on the hospital's existing HIPAA-eligible account, with logging kept inside covered paths.
Direct API calls on a BAA-covered configuration: a BAA arranged with Anthropic, which provisions a dedicated HIPAA-enabled organization.
Any API feature, including betas, from a HIPAA-enabled organization, because a signed BAA extends to every feature it can reach.
Direct API calls from the hospital's standard (non-HIPAA) organization, as long as PHI is scrubbed from the application's logs.
A consumer Claude plan paid for by the hospital, because a paid plan is covered by a BAA once the account owner accepts the terms.

questions.explanation: The course lists two shapes of HIPAA route. The first is direct API calls on a BAA-covered configuration, arranged with Anthropic, which provisions a dedicated HIPAA-enabled organization that enforces feature restrictions. The second is a cloud-mediated route via Bedrock or Vertex on the partner's existing HIPAA-eligible cloud account. Analogy: health insurance pays only at in-network clinics; a clinic outside the network, or a new treatment the plan hasn't approved yet, isn't covered just because you hold a card. The tempting beta-feature option fails because the BAA excludes Console, Workbench, beta features, and consumer plans.

distractor_explanations.C: The course says the BAA does not cover beta features, and not all API features are covered, so eligibility must be checked.
distractor_explanations.D: BAA coverage for direct API access comes through the dedicated HIPAA-enabled organization. Scrubbing logs doesn't bring a standard organization under the BAA.
distractor_explanations.E: The course says the BAA does not cover consumer plans, so PHI can't go there regardless of who pays.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A contractor's production workload runs on Claude via Amazon Bedrock GovCloud at FedRAMP High. To save setup time, developers propose running development and test against the commercial first-party endpoint with synthetic data, then switching endpoints at release. What does the course say about this plan?

options.text: Accept it if dev and test move to Claude Enterprise on AWS Marketplace, which carries the same FedRAMP authorization as GovCloud.
Accept it, provided the commercial endpoint is called through a VPN, with the network path defining the authorized boundary.
Rule it out: dev and test on the commercial endpoint while production uses the authorized one lets credentials and code patterns leak.
Accept it, because FedRAMP authorization applies only to the production path, and synthetic test data carries no impact level of its own.

questions.explanation: For FedRAMP, the course rules out any code path that calls an endpoint not on an authorized environment at the required impact level, and it calls out the split where dev and test hit the commercial endpoint while production hits the authorized one, because credentials and code patterns leak between them. Analogy: a trainee pilot who practices on a home simulator with a different cockpit layout builds reflexes, such as where each switch sits, that follow them into the real aircraft; the safe rule is to train in the same cockpit you will fly. The synthetic-data argument is tempting, but the risk is habits, credentials, and code patterns leaking between environments, not the data itself.

distractor_explanations.A: The course says Claude Enterprise on AWS Marketplace is not FedRAMP authorized, so this swap fixes nothing.
distractor_explanations.B: Authorization belongs to the cloud environment and impact level, not to how traffic reaches a commercial endpoint.
distractor_explanations.D: The course explicitly includes dev and test paths in what FedRAMP rules out, regardless of the data used.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team packages an MCP server built during an engagement as a reusable asset. Its tool scopes and the customer's directory paths are hardcoded in the server code, so each new install needs code edits. What does the course's packaging guidance require for an MCP server package?

options.text: Keep the scopes hardcoded for safety, and ship a README listing the exact lines that a new team should edit before installing the server.
Bundle the original customer's credentials with the server, so the next team can verify that it works before replacing them.
Document each tool input and let the installing team set scopes, credential references, and paths so that no install needs code edits.
Ship it as a set of loose scripts, one per tool, so each new team can copy only the scripts it needs and adapt them locally.

questions.explanation: An MCP server package should document each tool input and let the installing team set the scope, so it installs into a new environment without code edits. The checklist parameterizes scopes, credentials by reference, and per-customer paths, and documents expected inputs, scope boundaries, and handled failure modes.

distractor_explanations.A: Editing code per install is what packaging is meant to prevent. The installing team should set scope through configuration.
distractor_explanations.B: Credentials are passed by reference, never bundled. Shipping a customer's secrets is a security failure, not packaging.
distractor_explanations.D: The course calls shipping loose scripts instead of a template the most common version of the wrong approach; the next team copies and diverges them.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A company rolls out a remote MCP server for its cloud issue tracker to 40 developers. The tracker authorizes access per user. To spare everyone the browser sign-in, a team lead proposes one shared token for the whole team. Which approach fits the course's authentication guidance?

options.text: Have one administrator complete the sign-in, then copy the stored token to each teammate's machine so the browser step happens only once overall.
Move the server to stdio transport so that network authentication is not needed and the sign-in step disappears for the whole team.
Keep OAuth and accept the one-time browser sign-in per developer; each person's stored token then ties access to an individual, auditable identity.
Issue one shared token and have each developer set it as an environment variable, which skips the sign-in and keeps the secret out of the config file.

questions.explanation: For a remote service whose authorization is tied to user identity, the course prescribes OAuth: the server returns a 401, the client opens a browser sign-in, and the issued token is stored with no one copying a secret by hand. Its listed cost is a one-time setup step per user per service, which is the price of an auditable per-person identity. A shared or copied token removes that step but loses the identity the audit and authorization depend on.

distractor_explanations.A: The issued token belongs to the person who signed in, and copying it by hand is the manual credential handling that OAuth is meant to avoid.
distractor_explanations.B: Stdio fits local services governed by file-system permissions. The tracker is a remote SaaS service, so its transport and identity model stay the same.
distractor_explanations.D: Environment variables fix where a secret is stored, not whose identity it represents. A shared token makes every action look like one user, which defeats per-user authorization and audit.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: While on a customer engagement, a developer finds a one-line bug in an existing Claude Cookbook example and fixes it in the customer's fork. They want to send the fix upstream today. Which readiness item does the course put first?

options.text: The rights check: confirm you may contribute code carried over from the engagement, with prior work attributed, before technical review.
A different channel: send the fix to the repository of the tool the example uses, since the Cookbook does not accept fixes to examples.
A larger scope: bundle the fix with the customer's surrounding application so maintainers can see the fix running in its real context.
Nothing extra: a one-line fix is self-evidently correct, so it can be opened immediately and licensing can be raised if a maintainer asks.

questions.explanation: Licensing and attribution decide whether a contribution can be accepted at all, so the course puts the rights check before technical review, and code carried in from a customer engagement may have constraints on where it can go. Analogy: before a family recipe goes into a published community cookbook, you ask the relative who owns it; how short or tasty the recipe is doesn't matter if you didn't have permission to share it. The tempting option treats a one-line change as too small to need the check, but the gate is about provenance, not size, and an uncleared constraint should be escalated to the owner rather than contributed.

distractor_explanations.B: A fix to a Cookbook example belongs with that example. The tool's repository is for fixes to the tool itself.
distractor_explanations.C: A whole application doesn't fit a review built for one focused pattern; more scope slows review rather than helping it.
distractor_explanations.D: Size doesn't remove the licensing gate. Engagement code can carry constraints that block the merge regardless of size.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A reporting job sends the same 15,000-token instruction prefix, marked with `cache_control` on the default lifetime, once every two hours. Usage shows a cache write on every run and no cache reads. Which change best fits the course's caching economics?

options.text: Move the breakpoint to the end of the user message, so the cached prefix is longer and reaches a higher discount tier on reads.
Set `ttl: 1h` on the breakpoint so the entry lasts long enough, because the one-hour lifetime makes every later run a cheap cache read.
Remove the breakpoint here, since each run pays the write premium and the entry expires before it is read, so caching only adds cost.
Add three more breakpoints across the prefix, so that at least one shorter cached segment survives until the next run arrives.

questions.explanation: Cache writes cost more than base input (1.25x for the five-minute lifetime, 2x for one hour) and reads cost 0.1x, so caching only pays when reads outnumber writes within the lifetime. Analogy: a gym that charges a sign-up fee and cancels your membership after a month of no visits is a bad deal if you only go every two months, because you pay the fee every time and never enjoy the cheap visits. With a two-hour gap, both lifetimes expire before the next run. The one-hour option is tempting, but it raises the write price and still never produces a read.

distractor_explanations.A: There are no discount tiers by length, and a longer prefix that includes changing content would miss the cache anyway.
distractor_explanations.B: A two-hour gap outlasts the one-hour lifetime too, and one-hour writes cost 2x, so this makes each run more expensive.
distractor_explanations.D: Every segment has the same lifetime. More breakpoints add more writes without producing any reads two hours later.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A retailer runs a nightly job that classifies 30,000 product descriptions. Every request starts with the same 6,000-token instruction block and taxonomy, and nobody reviews results until morning. Which combination lowers cost most while fitting the workload?

options.text: Enable extended thinking at high effort, so each label is right first time and fewer requests need to be resubmitted next day.
Stream every request synchronously; streaming returns the first token sooner and so lowers the cost of each classification.
Use an orchestrator-worker design with five subagents, so the 30,000 descriptions are split and classified in parallel overnight.
Run it through the Message Batches API and cache the shared instruction prefix, so both discounts apply to every request.

questions.explanation: The course says batching and prompt caching compound when a non-urgent job reuses the same context: the batch discount (around 50%) lowers each request's cost, and caching lowers the cost of the repeated prefix inside each one. A scheduled job with a long fixed instruction block is the textbook case.

distractor_explanations.A: Thinking tokens are billed as output and are wasted on classification. It raises cost without fitting the task.
distractor_explanations.B: Streaming changes perceived latency for a waiting user. It doesn't lower the token bill, and nobody is waiting here.
distractor_explanations.C: Fan-out multiplies token use by roughly 15x. It buys parallel exploration, not cheaper classification of independent items.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team adds a `cache_control` breakpoint to a 600-token system prompt that is identical on every request. Usage shows no cache writes and no cache reads at all. The model is a current model with the typical threshold. What explains this?

options.text: Breakpoints only work on user messages, not on the system prompt, so the marker must be moved to the last user turn of the request.
The system prompt must be sent twice within five minutes before the cache activates, so early traffic shows no cache writes at all.
Caching needs the `ttl: 1h` option on short prefixes, with the default five-minute lifetime applying only to prefixes above 4,000 tokens.
The prefix is under the minimum cacheable length, about 1,024 tokens for most current models, so the breakpoint does nothing at all.

questions.explanation: Caching applies only above a minimum token threshold, which varies by model and is 1,024 tokens for most current models. A 600-token prompt sees no benefit however stable it is, so the breakpoint produces neither writes nor reads. Caching pays off most on long, fixed prefixes.

distractor_explanations.A: The course recommends caching stable system prompts and tools. Placement isn't the problem here; length is.
distractor_explanations.B: The first eligible request writes the cache immediately. There is no warm-up rule; the prefix is simply too short.
distractor_explanations.C: The lifetime option doesn't change whether caching applies. A minimum length threshold does, and this prefix is under it.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A summarization feature runs on Sonnet. A product manager wants to switch it to Haiku next sprint to cut costs, noting that Haiku is cheaper and faster. No eval has been run on Haiku yet. What does the course recommend?

options.text: Run the eval on Haiku first, and move down a tier only if it shows the quality drop is acceptable for this task, not just cheaper.
Switch now and watch user complaints; a production rollout is the quickest and most realistic way to learn whether Haiku is good enough.
Switch to Opus instead, because a more capable model finishes in fewer tokens and so typically costs less than Sonnet in practice.
Keep Sonnet permanently, because Sonnet is the required model for production workloads and moving off it is not recommended.

questions.explanation: The course's default is to start with Sonnet, move up only when an eval shows Sonnet missing the quality bar, and move down to Haiku only when an eval shows the quality regression is acceptable for the task. Model moves should be measured decisions, not cost-driven guesses.

distractor_explanations.B: This replaces measurement with incidents. The course makes the eval the instrument for any tier move.
distractor_explanations.C: A higher tier can cost less per task when it needs fewer tokens, but that must be measured, and moving up also needs eval evidence.
distractor_explanations.D: Sonnet is the default starting point, not a mandate. Moving down is fine when an eval shows quality holds.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team runs two workloads on one of the newest Claude models: an overnight job extracting an order number from 50,000 emails, and an agent that plans a multi-step database migration where each step depends on the last. Which TWO configurations follow the course? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Leave extended thinking off for the order-number extraction, since a lookup gains nothing from reasoning and the extra tokens would be wasted.
Set `budget_tokens: 4096` on the migration planner, since a fixed thinking budget is the supported way to control reasoning depth.
Enable thinking at high effort for the extraction job too; thinking tokens are billed at the input rate and cost little at volume.
Strip thinking blocks from the planner's history between tool calls, so the accumulated reasoning does not crowd the context window.
Enable adaptive thinking for the migration planner with effort matched to the problem's depth, and budget for the planning step, not per call.

questions.explanation: The course enables thinking for multi-step reasoning and agentic planning, with effort matched to depth and budgeted for the planning step, and leaves it off for mechanical or lookup tasks such as extraction. On current models depth is set by effort, not `budget_tokens`, and thinking tokens are billed as output.

distractor_explanations.B: `budget_tokens` is deprecated and returns a 400 on the newest models. Depth is tuned with the effort setting.
distractor_explanations.C: Thinking tokens cost the same as output tokens, and thinking does not improve mechanical extraction.
distractor_explanations.D: Thinking blocks must go back to the API unchanged in a tool loop. Stripping them breaks the signature check.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A formatting task must return a specific nested structure. Sonnet gets the structure right zero-shot; Haiku gets the content right but invents its own structure about a third of the time. The team wants Haiku's lower cost. What should they try first, per the course?

options.text: Turn on extended thinking at high effort for Haiku, the standard fix when output arrives in a structure the prompt did not ask for.
Add three more paragraphs describing the structure in detail, since a longer description is how a smaller model learns a new output format.
Add a couple of worked examples of the exact structure to Haiku's prompt and re-run the eval; examples can let a cheaper model do it.
Accept Sonnet as the only option; a model that fails zero-shot cannot be brought to the quality bar by any change to the prompt.

questions.explanation: Prompting mode and model choice are linked levers: a more capable model often succeeds zero-shot where a smaller one needs a few examples, and adding examples can let the cheaper model meet the bar. Analogy: an experienced cook plates a dish correctly from a verbal description, while a trainee gets it right once you show them a photo of the finished plate; the photo is cheaper than hiring a second head chef. The course's discipline is to try the cheapest model with the fewest examples that pass the eval. The longer-description option is tempting, but invented structure is exactly the failure few-shot examples fix.

distractor_explanations.A: Invented structure points to missing examples. Thinking adds output-priced tokens and is not the course's fix for format.
distractor_explanations.B: Description often fails to pin down exact structure, and longer prompts tend to produce longer outputs, not better structure.
distractor_explanations.D: The course says a smaller model often needs a few examples where a larger one succeeds zero-shot, so this gives up too early.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team's monthly Claude bill doubled after a feature launch. Their dashboards only show the total invoice, so nobody can say which step of the multi-step flow is responsible. What does the course recommend doing first?

options.text: Add caching breakpoints to every request; caching is the highest-leverage fix whatever the source of the cost increase turns out to be.
Instrument every call with input and output tokens, latency, and error rate, so the expensive step is found from data, not guessed.
Wait for next month's invoice to confirm the trend, because a single month of data cannot show whether the increase is real or just noise.
Move the whole flow down one model tier immediately; a cheaper model is the fastest way to bring any doubled bill back under control.

questions.explanation: Observability for a Claude system means recording token usage, latency, and error rate per call. Per-call data turns a high bill into a sortable table, and often reveals that one step accounts for most of the spend, which is where optimization effort should go.

distractor_explanations.A: Caching helps only stable, repeated prefixes. Without instrumentation, nobody knows whether those are the cost driver.
distractor_explanations.C: Waiting leaves the cause unknown. The course says to instrument from the start so the bill never arrives before the explanation.
distractor_explanations.D: Without per-call data this may cut the wrong step, and a tier move needs eval evidence that quality still holds.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A help-desk assistant runs every request on Opus. Telemetry shows about 90% of requests are short FAQ lookups that Sonnet answers at the quality bar on the eval, while 10% are complex multi-document analyses where only Opus passes. What does the course recommend?

options.text: Keep Opus for everything; one model is simpler to operate and keeps the complex requests reliably above the quality bar.
Move everything to Sonnet, because 90% of the traffic passes, and a 10% shortfall on the hard requests is an acceptable trade for the savings.
Have Opus classify each request first and then forward it, so the most capable model is the one that decides where each request goes.
Route requests, with a Sonnet default for most traffic and an Opus override for complex ones, picked on a cheap signal in each request.

questions.explanation: The course's production pattern is a default model plus an override: send the bulk of traffic to a balanced default and route specific request types to a larger or smaller model on a cheap signal such as task type or input length. Routing earns its cost when traffic is mixed, as it is here.

distractor_explanations.A: This pays top-tier rates on the 90% that a cheaper model already handles; the course routes mixed traffic.
distractor_explanations.B: The eval shows Sonnet failing the complex cases. The course steps down only where the quality bar still holds.
distractor_explanations.C: The router should be a cheap call or signal. Putting the top model in front of every request adds Opus cost to all traffic, including the 90%.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team is deciding between the default cache lifetime and `ttl: 1h` for several workloads with long, stable prefixes. Which TWO statements about cache lifetime economics are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A one-hour cache write costs 2x base input versus 1.25x for a five-minute write, so it pays off only when the longer life turns rewrites into reads.
Repeated content is discounted automatically on every request, even without a cache flag or a breakpoint, once the same prefix has been seen once.
Each cache hit refreshes the default five-minute lifetime, so a prefix that is read every couple of minutes stays warm without the one-hour option.
Choosing the one-hour lifetime also lowers the read price below 0.1x, which offsets the higher write cost on any workload with repeated prefixes.
Cache reads are billed at the same rate as uncached input tokens, so caching improves latency but leaves the token bill for each request unchanged.

questions.explanation: Writes carry a premium (1.25x for five minutes, 2x for one hour), reads cost about 0.1x, and the default lifetime is refreshed on every hit. The one-hour option is worth its higher write price only when gaps between requests exceed five minutes but stay under an hour. Analogy: a parking meter that resets every time you add a coin needs no long-stay ticket if you top it up often, while the pricier all-day ticket only pays if you would otherwise keep coming back to a meter that has already expired. The read-rate distractor tempts people who think caching only speeds things up, but reads are the main saving.

distractor_explanations.B: Caching must be turned on, through the automatic-mode flag or explicit breakpoints. Repeated content isn't discounted by default.
distractor_explanations.D: The read rate is the same either way. The one-hour option changes how long the entry lives and what the write costs.
distractor_explanations.E: Reads cost about 0.1x base input. The saving on the token bill is the main reason caching pays off on reused prefixes.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A pricing agent looks up supplier costs and drafts quotes. Occasionally the supplier tool returns an empty result or a unit cost of $0.00, and the agent drafts a quote anyway. Retrying the tool returns the same value. Where does the course place a human-in-the-loop check for this?

options.text: Only before the final send step, because a quote is reversible until it leaves the system, so earlier checks add delay with no real benefit.
After session end, by reviewing a sample of finished quotes each week; spot checks catch bad values more cheaply than pausing the agent.
Nowhere: more retries with exponential backoff and jitter will eventually return a valid unit cost from the supplier tool.
On unexpected output, pausing for review when a result is empty, flagged as an error, or out of bounds, since retries alone won't fix it.

questions.explanation: The course lists three insertion points: before a destructive call, after a planning step, and on unexpected output, meaning an error flag, an empty result, or a value outside expected bounds. That last one catches failure modes that retry logic alone will not resolve, like a repeated zero cost.

distractor_explanations.A: A check before sending helps, but the course names unexpected output as its own insertion point for failures retries won't fix.
distractor_explanations.B: A later audit finds the problem after quotes have gone out. The course places the check at the moment the odd value appears.
distractor_explanations.C: The value repeats on retry, so it is not transient. Retry logic alone cannot resolve this failure mode.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A clinical-documentation agent will run sessions lasting up to two hours and handles PHI under a HIPAA BAA. The team likes Claude Managed Agents because Anthropic would run the loop and the sandbox. Which wiring path fits the governing constraint?

options.text: Claude Managed Agents on Claude Platform on AWS, because billing through an AWS account brings the sessions under the AWS HIPAA program.
The Agent SDK or a raw loop on a BAA-covered configuration, since Managed Agents sessions are stored server-side and aren't BAA-eligible.
Claude Managed Agents with PHI removed from the agent definition, the one stored resource that falls outside BAA coverage.
Claude Managed Agents, because the long session length is the deciding factor and the managed sandbox is built for hours-long execution.

questions.explanation: Managed Agents sessions are stateful and stored server-side, which is why they are not currently eligible for Zero Data Retention or a HIPAA BAA. For PHI or ZDR workloads the course routes to the Agent SDK or a raw loop on a covered configuration. Analogy: a hotel offers to keep your luggage in its storeroom overnight, which is convenient, but if your employer's rule says sensitive files may never be left with a third party, the convenience doesn't matter and you keep the bag with you. The tempting choice is Managed Agents for the long sessions, but the governing constraint picks the path first.

distractor_explanations.A: Billing through AWS doesn't change that sessions are stored server-side. The course gives no such HIPAA path for Managed Agents.
distractor_explanations.C: The sessions themselves are stateful and stored server-side; the PHI would flow through them regardless of the agent definition.
distractor_explanations.D: Session length favors Managed Agents operationally, but the PHI constraint rules the path out before convenience gets a say.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team is assigning memory scopes to three agents: a document formatter that receives one file and terminates, a support agent that helps the same customer at daily check-ins for two weeks, and a coding assistant used in one multi-hour session that will not resume. Which TWO pairings are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Document formatter: no persistent memory (stateless), because each job is independent and has no earlier session to recall.
Two-week support agent: in-context memory, replaying every previous check-in in full so the agent keeps every detail.
Document formatter: summarized memory, so each new job starts with a condensed record of the files it has formatted before.
Multi-hour coding assistant: external storage, the right scope once a session runs too long for in-context memory to hold.
Two-week support agent: external storage, writing state to a database at session end and reading it back at the next check-in.

questions.explanation: Memory scope follows the shape of the session. Self-contained jobs run stateless. Agents that continue a thread with the same user across sessions need external storage read back at session start. A single session that won't resume can keep state in context, because nothing must outlive it.

distractor_explanations.B: Replaying all prior sessions inflates every call and eventually fills the window. State must persist outside the context.
distractor_explanations.C: A self-contained job has nothing to recall. Summaries add a step and a cost for no benefit.
distractor_explanations.D: A single session that won't continue fits in-context memory; nothing needs to survive a restart.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: An order-support agent's system prompt still describes a `refund_order` tool that was removed from the tool registration last month. In traces, Claude sometimes tells users a refund is being processed or tries to route toward a tool that no longer exists. Which loop-wiring checklist item is violated?

options.text: Tool-result pairing, because each refund attempt must be answered by a `tool_result` block with the matching ID before the next turn.
The system prompt isn't scoped to the task and the tools actually registered, so it describes a tool the agent no longer has.
The HITL insertion point, because a human checkpoint before refunds would stop Claude from describing a refund to the user.
Exit conditions: the loop has no stopping criterion, so Claude keeps searching for a refund tool until it hits the iteration limit.

questions.explanation: The course's loop wiring checklist requires that the system prompt name the task and the available tools, not describe tools the agent does not have, and that no unregistered tool be referenced in the prompt. A stale tool description invites Claude to promise or route toward actions it cannot take.

distractor_explanations.A: No `tool_use` for the missing tool is ever executed, so pairing isn't the problem. The prompt describes a tool that isn't there.
distractor_explanations.C: A checkpoint gates actions that happen. The defect is that the prompt advertises a capability that isn't registered.
distractor_explanations.D: The trace shows a prompt-registration mismatch, not a loop that fails to stop. Exit conditions are a separate checklist item.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A project's CLAUDE.md says `Never read files under /vendor/licensed/.` A developer delegates codebase research to the built-in Explore subagent, and its findings quote content from `/vendor/licensed/`. The main session has never broken the rule. What is the most likely explanation and fix?

options.text: Subagents inherit the parent's history but not its permissions, so the rule was lost at delegation; grant the subagent the same permission set.
Explore loads CLAUDE.md but treats project rules as optional hints, so the rule must be repeated in every delegation prompt to be enforced.
The CLAUDE.md file has grown too long and diluted the rule, so the fix is to shorten it until the main session and subagents both follow it.
Explore skips CLAUDE.md to stay fast, so the rule never reached it; use the general-purpose subagent or a custom one that loads the rules.

questions.explanation: The built-in Explore and Plan subagents skip CLAUDE.md and git status to keep research fast, while the general-purpose subagent loads both. A project rule therefore does not apply inside Explore. Analogy: a substitute teacher handed only today's worksheet won't know the class rule about phones, which lives in the binder on the regular teacher's desk; if the rule matters, give the substitute the binder. The course's fix is the general-purpose subagent or a custom one that loads the rules. The tempting history-versus-permissions option inverts the facts, since subagents inherit permissions but not history.

distractor_explanations.A: This is reversed: subagents don't inherit history but do inherit the permission context. The gap is CLAUDE.md loading.
distractor_explanations.B: Explore and Plan skip CLAUDE.md and git status entirely; the rule is absent from their context, not downgraded.
distractor_explanations.C: Dilution could explain a main-session lapse, but the main session obeys the rule. Explore simply never loaded the file.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team is deciding whether a new feature should be built as a workflow or as an agent. Which TWO signals point toward an agent, according to the course's decision table? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Errors are costly, so step-level guardrails matter and each step must be checked before the next one starts.
The goal and the tools can be specified, but the exact path through the work cannot be enumerated in advance.
The operations team requires observability with standard logging tools rather than transcript-level tooling.
Every run of the task follows the same sequence of steps, so the steps can be written down once and executed in order every time.
User inputs vary unpredictably in content and structure, so a fixed sequence would break whenever input left the expected path.

questions.explanation: The course chooses an agent when the goal and tools are known but the path cannot be enumerated, inputs vary unpredictably, and the task needs creative sequencing of tools. It chooses a workflow when steps can be enumerated in code, error cost demands step-level guardrails, standard observability is required, and every run follows the same sequence.

distractor_explanations.A: The course lists real error cost with step-level guardrails as a reason to choose a workflow.
distractor_explanations.C: Standard-tooling observability favors a workflow; agents need transcript-level tooling.
distractor_explanations.D: A repeatable, fixed sequence is the textbook case for a workflow, not an agent.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A travel-booking agent is registered with only `search_flights` and `get_fare`. When users ask it to reserve a seat, it sometimes replies that the seat is booked, even though no tool can make a booking. What does the course's tool-orchestration guidance say is happening?

options.text: A streaming defect: the booking confirmation is a partial message committed before `message_stop`, so the user sees a half-built reply.
Under-tooling: with too few tools the agent hallucinates a path or an incomplete result; once the gap is confirmed, add a booking tool.
A memory defect: the agent recalls bookings from an earlier session and repeats them, so the fix is to switch the agent to stateless memory.
Over-tooling: the two lookup tools have overlapping descriptions, so Claude's selection degrades and it guesses an outcome instead of calling one.

questions.explanation: The course warns about both directions. Over-tooling (many overlapping tools) produces erratic routing, while under-tooling forces the agent to hallucinate a path or return an incomplete result. The discipline is to start from the minimum set and add a tool once a specific capability gap is confirmed, as it is here.

distractor_explanations.A: Nothing in the scenario involves an interrupted stream. The agent states an outcome it has no tool to produce.
distractor_explanations.C: The agent claims bookings it never had the ability to make. That is a missing capability, not a memory leak.
distractor_explanations.D: Over-tooling means too many overlapping tools. Here a needed capability is missing entirely.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A single agent answers a typical vendor-research question in about 8,000 tokens. A team proposes a lead agent plus four subagents that each research separate vendor sites, with the lead synthesizing at the end. Using the course's reported multiplier, what should the team expect and decide?

options.text: Expect about 40,000 tokens (five agents at 8,000 each), so the design is worth it whenever the five contexts finish faster than the single agent.
Expect about 120,000 tokens (roughly 15x); adopt it only if the question splits into independent parts that benefit from parallel exploration.
Expect about 8,000 tokens in total; the subagents split the same work, so the token budget is divided among them rather than multiplied.
Expect about 120,000 tokens, and adopt it regardless of task shape, since multi-agent setups were reported to improve quality in general.

questions.explanation: Anthropic reports that an orchestrator-worker system uses roughly fifteen times the tokens of a normal chat, so an 8,000-token question costs on the order of 120,000. The course says the architecture works mainly because it buys more parallel computation, so it is worth it only when the task splits into independent parts. Analogy: hiring a lead and four researchers who each re-read the sources and write a full report, which the lead then reads and merges, multiplies the reading and writing far beyond five times one person's effort; you hire that team only when the work splits into parts people can do without waiting on each other. The near-miss option gets the number right and the decision wrong, because tightly coupled tasks gain nothing from fan-out.

distractor_explanations.A: The reported multiplier is roughly 15x, not 5x, because each context plus the synthesis pass spends its own tokens.
distractor_explanations.C: Each subagent spends its own tokens against its own context. The cost multiplies; it is not shared out.
distractor_explanations.D: The number is right, but the gain applies to parallelizable work. For tightly coupled tasks the multiplier buys nothing.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A pipeline asks Claude to rate each product review's sentiment. The ratings are correct, but responses come back as sentences such as `This review seems mostly positive.` while the downstream parser expects a JSON object. Per the course's diagnosis table, what is the prompt missing?

options.text: More descriptive guidance on what positive and negative reviews look like, so Claude is more confident in each rating it gives.
Extended thinking, so Claude can reason through each review in full first and then format its final answer as JSON for the parser.
A more specific system prompt, because the behavioral contract is too vague to hold Claude's role and scope steady across turns.
An output constraint, since the prompt never set the form, field names, or stopping point, so Claude returns plausible prose.

questions.explanation: The course's diagnosis table maps a wrong output shape (a sentence where a label or JSON was expected) to a missing output constraint, because the prompt never specified the form, field names, or stopping point. When the output must be machine-readable, structured output features are the stronger form of that constraint.

distractor_explanations.A: The ratings are already correct. Adding description lengthens the prompt without fixing the output shape.
distractor_explanations.B: Wrong shape is a missing constraint, not missing reasoning. Thinking adds cost and doesn't define the form.
distractor_explanations.C: That row covers drifting scope or tone. Here the content is right and only the shape is wrong.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A debugging assistant receives the user's Python file followed by pasted library documentation that also contains Python examples. Claude sometimes "fixes" lines that only appear in the documentation examples. Which prompt change does the course recommend?

options.text: Use official XML tag names from the API reference, because Claude ignores tag names that Anthropic has not documented.
Wrap each input in descriptive XML tags such as `<my_code>` and `<docs>`, so the boundary between code and documentation is clear.
Remove the documentation from the prompt; Claude handles reference material and user content poorly when both arrive in one request.
Add `Only fix the user's code` in bold at the top of the prompt; clearer and stronger wording keeps Claude away from the documentation.

questions.explanation: XML tags are the course's tool when a prompt mixes inputs with instructions, and its example is exactly this: code plus documentation look the same to Claude without tags. Descriptive names like `<my_code>` and `<docs>` make the boundary unambiguous; official tag names are not required.

distractor_explanations.A: The course says you don't need official tag names; descriptive names that match the content work best.
distractor_explanations.C: The documentation is useful context. Tags let both inputs coexist without being confused.
distractor_explanations.D: The course says clearer phrasing won't fix a boundary problem. The missing piece is structure that separates the inputs.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: An agent calls `fetch_policy_document` four times, adding about 2,400 tokens each. On turns 5 and 6 it starts choosing the wrong tool, and the session ends without a result. Which TWO actions address the root cause? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Rewrite the `apply_coverage_rule` description with sharper exclusion conditions; wrong-tool selection is a description problem at its root.
Prune each `fetch_policy_document` result once it has been used, so accumulated outputs stop crowding out the instructions about tool choice.
Increase `max_tokens` on each request, so Claude has more room to respond and can reach the correct tool before the session runs out.
Switch to a model with a larger context window, since a bigger window is the standard fix when a long agent session's context fills up.
Apply compaction before the session reaches the point where selection degrades, rather than waiting until the agent has already failed.

questions.explanation: Tool outputs consume context like any other input, and large results that are never pruned crowd out the system prompt and early instructions, so selection degrades after a fixed number of turns. Analogy: a hiker who stuffs every snack wrapper back into the backpack eventually can't find the trail map; the map was packed, but it is buried. The course's fix is to prune results after use and compact proactively before the ceiling. The tempting description rewrite fails because the course warns that context overflow is often misread as a tool-selection problem, so check the context first.

distractor_explanations.A: Selection that degrades after a fixed number of turns points to context filling, not to a schema defect.
distractor_explanations.C: `max_tokens` limits output length. It does nothing about tool outputs crowding the input context.
distractor_explanations.D: The course says increasing the window isn't the solution; decide what enters context and prune or summarize the rest.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: An internal policy assistant answers questions like `Compare the travel and expense rules for contractors and explain which one is stricter.` The policy documents change several times a week. Which retrieval approach does the course favor for this corpus and query shape?

options.text: Search across rounds (agentic search), which reads current files at query time and so suits a changing corpus and multi-step questions.
Load the full policy corpus into the system prompt on each request, since whole-corpus context removes the need for a retrieval step.
Fetch-once retrieval from a pre-built index; a static index is the most inspectable option, and staleness doesn't affect comparison questions.
Lexical keyword search only, because semantic retrieval cannot handle comparisons across two documents in the same question.

questions.explanation: The course contrasts two paths. Fetch-once retrieval from an index is inspectable but requires building and syncing that index, which suits a stable corpus with simple lookups. Search across rounds reads current files at query time and suits a changing corpus or multi-step questions, at the cost of more tokens and a less inspectable process.

distractor_explanations.B: This spends the context budget on everything for every question. Retrieval exists to supply only the relevant slice.
distractor_explanations.C: A frequently changing corpus makes an index costly to keep in sync, and multi-step comparisons need more than one pass.
distractor_explanations.D: The course pairs lexical with semantic matching for exact terms. It doesn't say semantic search fails on comparisons.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team running a long API-based coding agent has written its own compaction step using the summarizer prompt `Briefly summarize the session.` After each compaction the agent redoes finished work. They ask what the course documents for compaction on the API. What is the best answer?

options.text: Run `/compact` from the application, because the Claude Code command is the documented compaction mechanism for agents built on the API too.
Switch from compaction to clearing at each step, so a fresh context removes the stale summary that is causing work to be repeated.
Keep the summarizer as written and raise the context window; the repeated work comes from the window being too small to hold the summary.
Server-side compaction (beta) is the documented primary API strategy; a manual summarizer must preserve file paths, decisions, and errors.

questions.explanation: In the API the documented primary strategy is server-side compaction, a beta feature the platform performs for you when configured on the request; manual summarization is the client-side alternative. When you compact manually, the summarizer prompt decides what the agent knows next, so it must preserve file paths modified, decisions made, and errors and their resolutions. Analogy: a dishwasher's built-in program follows its own tested cycle, but if a roommate washes up by hand instead, the result depends entirely on the note you leave; a note that just says do the dishes leaves the pans soaking. The `/compact` option is tempting but belongs to Claude Code, not the API.

distractor_explanations.A: `/compact` is a Claude Code command. On the API the documented primary path is server-side compaction, or a summarizer you write.
distractor_explanations.B: Clearing drops everything, including the work state the agent needs. It makes repeated work worse, not better.
distractor_explanations.C: The summary is small; the problem is what it omits. An under-specified summarizer drops task-critical state.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team's CLAUDE.md includes a 400-line accessibility review checklist that applies only when someone asks for an accessibility audit, which happens in a small fraction of sessions. Which change does the course recommend for this checklist?

options.text: Move it into a Skill whose description matches accessibility-audit requests, so its full content loads only when such a request arrives.
Keep it in CLAUDE.md; content there is cached after the first session and adds no cost to the sessions that don't use it.
Paste it into the conversation at the start of each audit, since in-context instructions persist across sessions once they have been sent.
Turn it into a PreToolUse hook, because hooks are Claude Code's mechanism for loading task-specific instructions on demand.

questions.explanation: A Skill loads its full instructions only when a request matches its description; at startup only its name and description load. CLAUDE.md loads every session regardless of task, so a large, rarely used checklist adds fixed overhead and dilutes the rules that matter. Task-specific procedures like this belong in a Skill.

distractor_explanations.B: CLAUDE.md loads into every session unconditionally, a fixed overhead regardless of the task, and it dilutes other rules.
distractor_explanations.C: In-context instructions grow with session length and don't survive the session's end.
distractor_explanations.D: Hooks run scripts at lifecycle events and add no instructions to context. On-demand instructions are what Skills provide.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A platform team is setting up three MCP integrations: a SaaS project tracker that authorizes each user individually, an internal reporting API called under a service account, and a local tool that reads files on the developer's machine. Which TWO pairings follow the course? (Select TWO.)

options.text: SaaS tracker with user identity: OAuth, where the server returns a 401, the client starts a browser sign-in, and a token is issued and stored.
Internal reporting API: an OAuth browser sign-in for each developer, since a remote service should authenticate individual users.
Internal reporting API: the service-account key written in `.mcp.json` headers, so each teammate who clones the repo can connect at once.
Local file tool: stdio transport with no network authentication, where file-system permissions and deny rules in settings form the governance layer.
Local file tool: a bearer token sent on each call, because settings have no way to govern a server without network authentication.

questions.explanation: The course matches auth to service type. Remote services with user identity use OAuth: a 401 triggers a browser sign-in and the issued token is stored. Remote services with service identity use an API key in an environment variable, never in committed config. Local services run over stdio with no network auth, governed by file-system permissions and deny rules.

distractor_explanations.B: A service-account integration uses an API key passed through an environment variable, not a per-user sign-in.
distractor_explanations.C: A key must never be committed to config. It lives in the environment and the config holds only a variable reference.
distractor_explanations.E: A local stdio server needs no network credential; the security boundary is the file-system permission model.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: An MCP server for a document store should let clients pull a list of all available documents, and also pull any single document's content by its ID, directly into context without the model making a tool call. Which MCP primitives fit?

options.text: Two tools, `list_documents` and `get_document`; tools are the only primitive that can return data from the server to the client.
A templated resource for the list and a direct resource per document, with each document's fixed ID making its address a direct one.
Prompts: one prompt that lists the documents and a second that returns content, since prompts are the primitive for fixed server content.
Resources: a direct resource with a fixed address for the document list, and a templated resource whose address takes the document ID.

questions.explanation: An MCP resource is read-only data the client fetches by address and places into context directly. A direct resource has a fixed address for parameterless data, such as a document list; a templated resource puts a parameter in the address, such as a document ID. Resource support varies by client, so confirm the client can inject resources.

distractor_explanations.A: Tools work, but the model must call them. Resources let the client place known data in context directly.
distractor_explanations.B: This swaps the forms: a direct resource takes no parameters, and an address with a parameter is a templated resource.
distractor_explanations.C: A prompt is a vetted instruction template invoked by name, not a way to fetch data by address.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: An agent has `quote_domestic_shipping` and `quote_international_shipping` with identical input schemas. After three rounds of adding exclusion conditions, the descriptions are long and Claude still mixes them up on border cases such as overseas territories. What does the course recommend next?

options.text: Set `tool_choice` to force `quote_international_shipping` on border cases, so the model doesn't have to decide between the two.
Mark each parameter in both schemas as required, so the stricter input schemas force Claude to tell the two shipping tools apart.
Merge them into one shipping-quote tool with a type parameter, since descriptions that can't be cleanly separated signal a merge.
Add a fourth round of exclusion conditions with worked examples; a long enough description eventually separates any two tools.

questions.explanation: When two tools share a signature, routing collapses to the description, and the fix is one sentence on when to use each tool and one on when not to. If even exclusion conditions can't cleanly separate them, the course says merge them into one tool with a type parameter.
